newsitem.title: UK: Dlr firm in late Europe but intervention fears cap.
newsitem.headline: Dlr firm in late Europe but intervention fears cap.

text.p: The dollar was sturdy in late Europe but unable to gain a firm foothold above 1.80 marks as the market remained nervous of central bank intervention to rein it in.

In a keenly-awaited statement, the German government today reminded the markets that the Group of Seven said in February -- when dollar/mark traded down in the mid-1.60s -- that the mark's appreciation had been fully corrected.
But the U.S. unit shrugged off that comment, plus Bonn's assertion that it was in close contact with its G7 partners on forex and there was no need to dramatise currency developments.
"It's an invitation to sell more marks," said Nick Parsons, forex strategist at Banque Paribas in London.
"This is not just a phenomenon which is driven by dollar strength, this is a period of all-round mark weakness and reflects insecurity about the German economy and EMU."

The dollar hit a European session high of 1.8010 marks despite the statement, but had returned to 1.7968/78 by 1511 GMT. That compared with Tuesday's close here of 1.8025/30 and the 71-month peak of 1.8040 it scaled yesterday.
Though the immediate reaction to Bonn's words was dismissive, traders said intervention remained a real risk.
"I think they'll intervene -- I think they're telling you not to get too long of dollars around here," said Nick Probert, head of spot trading at Bank of America in London.
Analysts said central bank action was perhaps the only way now to staunch the dollar's inexorable rise. If none appeared, the dollar would push decisively above 1.80 marks, they said.
"The market is unimpressed with verbal intervention now to be honest, we've heard so much," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
Dollar/yen had a good day, breaching 116 yen for the first time since early June.
The dollar stood at 116.16/19 yen at 1538 GMT, up from Tuesday's late European level of 115.88/98, and well above the 113.73/83 level at which it began the week.
Traders talked of heavy buying of dollar/yen by a major U.S. hedge fund, and said 118 was now a realistic near-term target.
The options market provided a graphic illustration of the shift in dollar/yen sentiment, with the market preference for yen calls shrinking dramatically.
However, analysts warned that forthcoming Japanese trade figures could cast a cloud over dollar/yen as they revealed further widening in Japan's surplus.
A Reuters poll of economists foresees the surplus ballooning to 1.1 trillion yen in June from May's 738.3 billion.
The U.S. May trade deficit, by contrast, is expected to grow to $9.2 billion from $8.4 billion last time.

Figures out today showed U.S. CPI up 0.1 percent in June, slightly below the 0.2 generally expected, though the Labor Department warned that inflation -- while currently in check -- was unlikely to stay at such low levels.
June industrial production showed a rise of 0.3 percent versus the 0.2 increase expected, with capacity utilisation at 83.5 compared to the consensus forecast of 83.6.
"The U.S. data were more or less neutral for the dollar, with quite a mild CPI and fairly moderate industrial production," said Sonja Gibbs, market strategist at Nomura International.
Elswhere, the mark firmed against the yen to 64.64/66 from late Tuesday's level of 64.23/26 while mark/Swiss climbed to 82.46/47 centimes from 82.07/09.
Dollar/Swiss franc rose to 1.4824/34 from 1.4800/10 late yesterday.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
